query: For lightweight high-entropy alloys intended for weight-critical aerospace and rail-transport applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability—or inability—to combine low density with mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, the observations predicted relative to a baseline alloy, the conditions under which the hypothesis should cease to hold, the existing observations that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: If the Al fraction in the composition of a lightweight high-entropy alloy surpasses a critical threshold, a continuous Al2O3-rich surface oxide layer forms under high-temperature or corrosive conditions, thereby providing and simultaneously maintaining low density, mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: A baseline lightweight high-entropy alloy with sub-critical Al content insufficient for forming a robust protective oxide layer.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the Al fraction in the HEA composition above and below the hypothesized critical value, then evaluate microstructure, oxidation/corrosion behavior, and mechanical properties.
generation.conditions: Perform thermogravimetric tests at elevated temperatures (up to ~800 °C) in air and immersions in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution; assess mechanical strength at ambient and elevated temperatures to correlate with oxide formation.
generation.structural_mediator: The dense Al2O3-rich passivation layer that forms when Al content is sufficiently high and effectively migrates to the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: Elevated Al content drives the enrichment of the alloy surface by Al, leading to a dense, stable Al2O3 scale that inhibits both corrosion and high-temperature oxidation, while solid solution strengthening maintains mechanical strength alongside low density.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to an Al-deficient baseline alloy, samples above the critical Al fraction will exhibit significantly reduced oxidation rates and corrosion current densities while retaining comparable or improved hardness/tensile strength and lower density.
generation.baseline: An analogous HEA with lower Al concentration that does not consistently form a protective Al2O3 surface film, demonstrating higher corrosion rates, faster oxidation kinetics, and reduced mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: If Al content is excessively high, secondary fragile phases may form or density may increase, diminishing the alloy’s combined property advantage and indicating no further benefit.
generation.uncertainty: The precise Al threshold depends on secondary alloying elements, processing routes, and thermomechanical treatments, necessitating experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate a series of at least four compositional variants with stepped Al contents (e.g., 0, 5, 10, and 15 at%). Expose them to identical processing, then conduct thermogravimetric tests in air at ~800 °C for a fixed duration, followed by corrosion measurements in 3.5 wt% NaCl. Characterize mechanical behavior (such as hardness/tensile strength) and surface oxide morphology/composition.
measurements: Weight gain/loss over time during oxidation (thermogravimetric analysis)
Corrosion current density and potential from electrochemical polarization tests
Surface oxide composition and morphology (electron microscopy, XRD)
Hardness or tensile strength at room and elevated temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If higher-Al variants fail to display enhanced oxidation/corrosion resistance and mechanical performance beyond that of the baseline alloy, or if the protective Al2O3 scale is not consistently detected, then the proposed mechanism is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this study, the oxidation behavior of the FeNiCuAlCr, FeNiCuAlCo, and FeNiCuAlMn high-entropy alloys (HEAs) was investigated in air at 900 °C, and their corrosion resistance in 3.5% NaCl solution was evaluated using potentiodynamic polarization and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS). The following conclusions were drawn:(1)The oxidation kinetics of the FeNiCuAlCr, FeNiCuAlCo, and FeNiCuAlMn HEAs in air at 900 °C follow a parabolic relationship. Among them, the FeNiCuAlCr HEA exhibited excellent oxidation resistance, with a low mass gain of 0.83 mg/cm2 after 108 h of exposure at 900 °C.(2)The outer oxidation layer of the FeNiCuAlCr HEA formed a dense and continuous Al2O3 and Cr2O3 layer, which provided effective protection for the substrate. In contrast, for the FeNiCuAlCo and FeNiCuAlMn HEAs, prolonged oxidation and increased high-temperature internal stress led to the partial peeling and wrinkling of the oxide scale at the interface between the scale and the alloy.(3)The electrochemical analysis revealed that the FeNiCuAlCr HEA possesses a high corrosion potential (Ecorr = −0.21 V) and a low corrosion current density (Icorr = 45.7 μA/cm2). However, the strong HEA films mentioned above suffer from low ductility in general. How to balance the strength and ductility of amorphous HEA films is important for their applications in the field of flexible microelectronic devices and mechanical metamaterials. In addition, seeking a high-performance HEA film with low density and corrosion resistance is of great significance for their applications in extreme conditions. In these cases, it is crucial to develop a high hardness, high strength–ductility synergy, and excellent corrosion resistance of amorphous lightweight high entropy alloy film. In this work, the lightweight AlTiVNb HEA film was prepared by magnetron sputtering, and the microstructure, mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance were investigated.

chosen.conditions: High-temperature oxidation in air (up to ~800 °C) and immersion in 3.5 wt% NaCl
chosen.why: Varying Al content in lightweight high-entropy alloys under well-defined heat treatment and corrosive environments provides a direct test of whether a protective Al-rich surface layer is responsible for maintaining mechanical strength, low density, and corrosion-oxidation resistance. Standard metallurgical characterization methods can confirm if the hypothesized surface mechanism is valid. A breakdown in these behaviors upon changes in Al content, or lack of any protective oxide formation, would falsify the hypothesis.
